title: Present continuous, and when not to use it
goal: Use -ing for now, and stop saying “I am having a car”
intro: The present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) is for actions happening now or around now, and for plans. But some verbs describe states, not actions, and almost never take -ing: know, understand, like, want, need, believe, own, have (= own). “I am having a doubt” and “I am knowing him” are classic Indian-English mistakes.

examples: I’m talking to a client right now.
She’s studying for her exams this month.

rules.rule: State verbs stay simple: know, understand, believe, like, love, hate, want, need, prefer, mean, own, belong, seem.
“have” = own is simple; “have” = eat, take, enjoy can be -ing.
examples: I have a question. / I have a car.
We’re having dinner. / We’re having fun.

mistakes.why: “Have” for owning is not used with -ing. And “doubt” means you don’t believe something; for asking, say “question”.

mistakes.wrong: I am knowing him since college.
mistakes.right: I have known him since college.

ex.q: Can I call you back? I ___ right now.
She ___ a new flat in Pune.
We ___ lunch. Can we talk later?
I am having one small doubt about the report.
ex.fixed: I have a quick question about the report.

ex.q: He is liking his new job.

ex.a: I'm working from home this week.

ex.q: Correct this: “I am having a doubt about this.”
a: I have a question about this
I have a doubt about this

talk: Tell the coach what you’re doing these days (your projects, what you’re learning) and what you’re doing this weekend. Then say two things you know or want, without -ing.
